Plot of the sharp blades, or the field of heroes, (⟦10.2.16|삼하 2:16⟧). After the battle of Gilboa, so fatal to Saul and his house, David, as divinely directed, took up his residence in Hebron, and was there anointed king over Judah. Among the fugitives from Gilboa was Ish-bosheth, the only surviving son of Saul, whom Abner, Saul’s uncle, took across the Jordan to Mahanaim, and there had him proclaimed king. Abner gathered all the forces at his command and marched to Gibeon, with the object of wresting Judah from David. Joab had the command of David’s army of trained men, who encamped on the south of the pool, which was on the east of the hill on which the town of Gibeon was built, while Abner’s army lay on the north of the pool. Abner proposed that the conflict should be decided by twelve young men engaging in personal combat on either side. So fiercely did they encounter each other that “they caught every man his fellow by the head, and thrust his sword in his fellow’s side; so they fell down together: wherefore that place was called Helkath-hazzurim.” The combat of the champions was thus indecisive, and there followed a severe general engagement between the two armies, ending in the total rout of the Israelites under Abner. The general result of this battle was that “David waxed stronger and stronger, and the house of Saul waxed weaker and weaker” (⟦10.3.1|삼하 3:1⟧).

Derived from the Saxon helan, to cover; hence the covered or the invisible place. In Scripture there are three words so rendered:
1. Sheol, occurring in the Old Testament sixty-five times. This word sheol is derived from a root-word meaning “to ask,” “demand;” hence insatiableness (⟦20.30.15|잠 30:15⟧, ⟦20.30.16|16⟧). It is rendered “grave” thirty-one times (⟦1.37.35|창 37:35⟧; ⟦1.42.38|42:38⟧; ⟦1.44.29|44:29⟧, ⟦1.44.31|31⟧; ⟦9.2.6|삼상 2:6⟧, etc.). The Revisers have retained this rendering in the historical books with the original word in the margin, while in the poetical books they have reversed this rule.
 In thirty-one cases in the Authorized Version this word is rendered “hell,” the place of disembodied spirits. The inhabitants of sheol are “the congregation of the dead” (⟦20.21.16|잠 21:16⟧). It is (a) the abode of the wicked (⟦4.16.33|민 16:33⟧; ⟦18.24.19|욥 24:19⟧; ⟦19.9.17|시 9:17⟧; ⟦19.31.17|31:17⟧, etc.); (b) of the good (⟦19.16.10|시 16:10⟧; ⟦19.30.3|30:3⟧; ⟦19.49.15|49:15⟧; ⟦19.86.13|86:13⟧, etc.).
 Sheol is described as deep (⟦18.11.8|욥 11:8⟧), dark (10:21, 22), with bars (17:16). The dead “go down” to it (⟦4.16.30|민 16:30⟧, ⟦4.16.33|33⟧; ⟦26.31.15|겔 31:15⟧, ⟦26.31.16|16⟧, ⟦26.31.17|17⟧).
2. The Greek word hades of the New Testament has the same scope of signification as sheol of the Old Testament. It is a prison (⟦60.3.19|벧전 3:19⟧), with gates and bars and locks (⟦40.16.18|마 16:18⟧; ⟦66.1.18|계 1:18⟧), and it is downward (⟦40.11.23|마 11:23⟧; ⟦42.10.15|눅 10:15⟧).
 The righteous and the wicked are separated. The blessed dead are in that part of hades called paradise (⟦42.23.43|눅 23:43⟧). They are also said to be in Abraham’s bosom (⟦42.16.22|눅 16:22⟧).
3. Gehenna, in most of its occurrences in the Greek New Testament, designates the place of the lost (⟦40.23.33|마 23:33⟧). The fearful nature of their condition there is described in various figurative expressions (⟦40.8.12|마 8:12⟧; ⟦40.13.42|13:42⟧; ⟦40.22.13|22:13⟧; ⟦40.25.30|25:30⟧; ⟦42.16.24|눅 16:24⟧, etc.).
(Heb. kob’a), a cap for the defence of the head (⟦9.17.5|삼상 17:5⟧, ⟦9.17.38|38⟧). In the New Testament the Greek equivalent is used (⟦49.6.17|엡 6:17⟧; ⟦52.5.8|살전 5:8⟧).
Strong, father of Eliab, who was “captain of the children of Zebulun” (⟦4.1.9|민 1:9⟧; ⟦4.2.7|2:7⟧).
(Heb. ‘ezer ke-negdo; i.e., “a help as his counterpart” = a help suitable to him), a wife (⟦1.2.18|창 2:18⟧).

(⟦46.12.28|고전 12:28⟧) may refer to help (i.e., by interpretation) given to him who speaks with tongues, or more probably simply help which Christians can render to one another, such as caring for the poor and needy, etc.

Of a garment, the fringe of a garment. The Jews attached much importance to these, because of the regulations in ⟦4.15.38|민 15:38⟧, ⟦4.15.39|39⟧. These borders or fringes were in process of time enlarged so as to attract special notice (⟦40.23.5|마 23:5⟧). The hem of Christ’s garment touched (9:20; 14:36; ⟦42.8.44|눅 8:44⟧).

Faithful.
1. ⟦11.4.31|왕상 4:31⟧; ⟦13.2.6|대상 2:6⟧, a son of Zerah, noted for his wisdom.
2. Grandson of Samuel (⟦13.6.33|대상 6:33⟧; ⟦13.15.17|15:17⟧), to whom the 88th Psalm probably was inscribed. He was one of the “seers” named in ⟦14.29.14|대하 29:14⟧, ⟦14.29.30|30⟧, and took a leading part in the administration of the sacred services.
A Kenite (⟦13.2.55|대상 2:55⟧), the father of the house of Rechab.

1. Heb. rosh (⟦28.10.4|호 10:4⟧; rendered “gall” in ⟦5.29.18|신 29:18⟧; ⟦5.32.32|32:32⟧; ⟦19.69.21|시 69:21⟧; ⟦24.9.15|렘 9:15⟧; ⟦24.23.15|23:15⟧; “poison,” ⟦18.20.16|욥 20:16⟧; “venom,” ⟦5.32.33|신 32:33⟧). “Rosh is the name of some poisonous plant which grows quickly and luxuriantly; of a bitter taste, and therefore coupled with wormwood (⟦5.29.18|신 29:18⟧; ⟦25.3.19|애 3:19⟧). Hence it would seem to be not the hemlock cicuta, nor the colocynth or wild gourd, nor lolium darnel, but the poppy so called from its heads” (Gesenius, Lex.).
2. Heb. la’anah, generally rendered “wormwood” (q.v.), ⟦5.29.18|신 29:18⟧, Text 17; ⟦20.5.4|잠 5:4⟧; ⟦24.9.15|렘 9:15⟧; ⟦24.23.15|23:15⟧. Once it is rendered “hemlock” (⟦30.6.12|암 6:12⟧; R.V., “wormwood”). This Hebrew word is from a root meaning “to curse,” hence the accursed.

Common in later times among the Jews in Palestine (⟦40.23.37|마 23:37⟧; ⟦42.13.34|눅 13:34⟧). It is noticeable that this familiar bird is only mentioned in these passages in connection with our Lord’s lamentation over the impenitence of Jerusalem.

One of the cities of Mesopotamia destroyed by sennacherib (⟦12.18.34|왕하 18:34⟧; ⟦12.19.13|19:13⟧). It is identified with the modern Anah, lying on the right bank of the Euphrates, not far from Sepharvaim.
Favour of Hadad, the name of a Levite after the Captivity (⟦15.3.9|스 3:9⟧).

A well or stream.
1. A royal city of the Canaanites taken by Joshua (12:17).
2. The youngest son of Gilead (⟦4.26.32|민 26:32⟧; ⟦4.27.1|27:1⟧).
3. The second son of Asher (⟦13.4.6|대상 4:6⟧).
4. One of David’s heroes (⟦13.11.36|대상 11:36⟧).

My delight is in her.
1. The wife of Hezekiah and mother of king Manasseh (⟦12.21.1|왕하 21:1⟧).
2. A symbolical name of Zion, as representing the Lord’s favour toward her (⟦23.62.4|사 62:4⟧).

1. Heb. ‘eseb, any green plant; herbage (⟦1.1.11|창 1:11⟧, ⟦1.1.12|12⟧, ⟦1.1.29|29⟧, ⟦1.1.30|30⟧; ⟦1.2.5|2:5⟧; ⟦1.3.18|3:18⟧, etc.); comprehending vegetables and all green herbage (⟦30.7.1|암 7:1⟧, ⟦30.7.2|2⟧).
2. Yarak, green; any green thing; foliage of trees (⟦12.19.26|왕하 19:26⟧; ⟦19.37.2|시 37:2⟧); a plant; herb (⟦5.11.10|신 11:10⟧).
3. Or, meaning “light” In ⟦23.26.19|사 26:19⟧ it means “green herbs;” in ⟦12.4.39|왕하 4:39⟧ probably the fruit of some plant.
4. Merorim, plural, “bitter herbs,” eaten by the Israelites at the Passover (⟦2.12.8|출 12:8⟧; ⟦4.9.11|민 9:11⟧). They were bitter plants of various sorts, and referred symbolically to the oppression in Egypt.

In Egypt herdsmen were probably of the lowest caste. Some of Joseph’s brethren were made rulers over Pharaoh’s cattle (⟦1.47.6|창 47:6⟧, ⟦1.47.17|17⟧). The Israelites were known in Egypt as “keepers of cattle;” and when they left it they took their flocks and herds with them (⟦2.12.38|출 12:38⟧). Both David and Saul came from “following the herd” to occupy the throne (⟦9.9.1|삼상 9장⟧; ⟦9.11.5|11:5⟧; ⟦19.78.70|시 78:70⟧). David’s herd-masters were among his chief officers of state. The daughters also of wealthy chiefs were wont to tend the flocks of the family (⟦1.29.9|창 29:9⟧; ⟦2.2.16|출 2:16⟧). The “chief of the herdsmen” was in the time of the monarchy an officer of high rank (⟦9.21.7|삼상 21:7⟧; comp. ⟦13.27.29|대상 27:29⟧). The herdsmen lived in tents (⟦23.38.12|사 38:12⟧; ⟦24.6.3|렘 6:3⟧); and there were folds for the cattle (⟦4.32.16|민 32:16⟧), and watch-towers for the herdsmen, that he might therefrom observe any coming danger (⟦33.4.8|미 4:8⟧; ⟦34.3.8|나 3:8⟧).

Sun.
1. “Mount Heres” (⟦7.1.35|삿 1:35⟧), Heb. Har-heres, i.e., “sun-mountain;” probably identical with Irshemesh in ⟦6.19.41|수 19:41⟧.
2. ⟦23.19.18|사 19:18⟧, marg.

From a Greek word signifying (1) a choice, (2) the opinion chosen, and (3) the sect holding the opinion. In the Acts of the Apostles (5:17; 15:5; 24:5, 14; 26:5) it denotes a sect, without reference to its character. Elsewhere, however, in the New Testament it has a different meaning attached to it. Paul ranks “heresies” with crimes and seditions (⟦48.5.20|갈 5:20⟧). This word also denotes divisions or schisms in the church (⟦46.11.19|고전 11:19⟧). In ⟦56.3.10|딛 3:10⟧ a “heretical person” is one who follows his own self-willed “questions,” and who is to be avoided. Heresies thus came to signify self-chosen doctrines not emanating from God (2 Pet. 2:1).

Mercury, a Roman Christian to whom Paul sends greetings (⟦45.16.1|롬 16장⟧: 14). Some suppose him to have been the author of the celebrated religious romance called The Shepherd, but it is very probable that that work is the production of a later generation.

Mercury-born, at one time Paul’s fellow-labourer in Asia Minor, who, however, afterwards abandoned him, along with one Phygellus, probably on account of the perils by which they were beset (⟦55.1.15|딤후 1:15⟧).

A peak, the eastern prolongation of the Anti-Lebanon range, reaching to the height of about 9,200 feet above the Mediterranean. It marks the north boundary of Palestine (⟦5.3.8|신 3:8⟧, ⟦5.3.4|4⟧:48; ⟦6.11.3|수 11:3⟧, ⟦6.11.17|17⟧; 13:11; 12:1), and is seen from a great distance. It is about 40 miles north of the Sea of Galilee. It is called “the Hermonites” (⟦19.42.6|시 42:6⟧) because it has more than one summit. The Sidonians called it Sirion, and the Amorites Shenir (⟦5.3.9|신 3:9⟧; ⟦22.4.8|아 4:8⟧). It is also called Baal-hermon (⟦7.3.3|삿 3:3⟧; ⟦13.5.23|대상 5:23⟧) and Sion (⟦5.4.48|신 4:48⟧). There is every probability that one of its three summits was the scene of the transfiguration (q.v.). The “dew of Hermon” is referred to (⟦19.89.1|시 89편⟧: 12). Its modern name is Jebel-esh-Sheikh, “the chief mountain.” It is one of the most conspicuous mountains in Palestine or Syria. “In whatever part of Palestine the Israelite turned his eye northward, Hermon was there, terminating the view. From the plain along the coast, from the Jordan valley, from the heights of Moab and Gilead, from the plateau of Bashan, the pale, blue, snow-capped cone forms the one feature in the northern horizon.”
 Our Lord and his disciples climbed this “high mountain apart” one day, and remained on its summit all night, “weary after their long and toilsome ascent.” During the night “he was transfigured before them; and his face did shine as the sun.” The next day they descended to Caesarea Philippi.
(⟦19.42.6|시 42:6⟧, ⟦19.42.7|7⟧) = “the Hermons”, i.e., the three peaks or summits of Hermon, which are about a quarter of a mile apart.

Son of Aristobulus and Bernice, and grandson of Herod the Great. He was made tetrarch of the provinces formerly held by Lysanias II., and ultimately possessed the entire kingdom of his grandfather, Herod the Great, with the title of king. He put the apostle James the elder to death, and cast Peter into prison (⟦42.3.1|눅 3:1⟧; ⟦44.12.1|행 12:1⟧). On the second day of a festival held in honour of the emperor Claudius, he appeared in the great theatre of Caesarea. “The king came in clothed in magnificent robes, of which silver was the costly brilliant material. It was early in the day, and the sun’s rays fell on the king, so that the eyes of the beholders were dazzled with the brightness which surrounded him. Voices here and there from the crowd exclaimed that it was the apparition of something divine. And when he spoke and made an oration to them, they gave a shout, saying, ’It is the voice of a god, and not of a man.’ But in the midst of this idolatrous ostentation an angel of God suddenly smote him. He was carried out of the theatre a dying man.” He died (A.D. 44) of the same loathsome malady which slew his grandfather (⟦44.12.21|행 12:21⟧), in the fifty-fourth year of his age, having reigned four years as tetrarch and three as king over the whole of Palestine. After his death his kingdom came under the control of the prefect of Syria, and Palestine was now fully incorporated with the empire.

The son of Herod Agrippa I. and Cypros. The emperor Claudius made him tetrarch of the provinces of Philip and Lysanias, with the title of king (⟦44.25.13|행 25:13⟧; ⟦44.26.2|26:2⟧, ⟦44.26.7|7⟧). He enlarged the city of Caesarea Philippi, and called it Neronias, in honour of Nero. It was before him and his sister that Paul made his defence at Caesarea (⟦44.25.12|행 25:12⟧). He died at Rome A.D. 100, in the third year of the emperor Trajan.

A Jewish political party who sympathized with (⟦41.3.6|막 3:6⟧; ⟦41.12.13|12:13⟧; Matt, 22:16; ⟦42.20.20|눅 20:20⟧) the Herodian rulers in their general policy of government, and in the social customs which they introduced from Rome. They were at one with the Sadducees in holding the duty of submission to Rome, and of supporting the Herods on the throne. (Comp. ⟦41.8.15|막 8:15⟧; ⟦40.16.6|마 16:6⟧.)

(⟦40.14.3|마 14:3⟧; ⟦41.6.17|막 6:17⟧; ⟦42.3.19|눅 3:19⟧), the daughter of Aristobulus and Bernice. While residing at Rome with her husband Herod Philip I. and her daughter, Herod Antipas fell in with her during one of his journeys to that city. She consented to leave her husband and become his wife. Some time after, Herod met John the Baptist, who boldly declared the marriage to be unlawful. For this he was “cast into prison,” in the castle probably of Machaerus (q.v.), and was there subsequently beheaded.
A Christian at Rome whom Paul salutes and calls his “kinsman” (⟦45.16.11|롬 16:11⟧).

(⟦41.6.17|막 6:17⟧), the son of Herod the Great by Mariamne, the daughter of Simon, the high priest. He is distinguished from another Philip called “the tetrarch.” He lived at Rome as a private person with his wife Herodias and his daughter Salome.

The son of Herod the Great and Cleopatra of Jerusalem. He was “tetrarch” of Batanea, Iturea, Trachonitis, and Auranitis. He rebuilt the city of Caesarea Philippi, calling it by his own name to distinguish it from the Caesarea on the sea-coast which was the seat of the Roman government. He married Salome, the daughter of Herodias (⟦40.16.13|마 16:13⟧; ⟦41.8.27|막 8:27⟧; ⟦42.3.1|눅 3:1⟧).

(⟦40.2.1|마 2:1⟧; ⟦42.1.5|눅 1:5⟧; ⟦44.23.35|행 23:35⟧), the son of Antipater, an Idumaean, and Cypros, an Arabian of noble descent. In the year B.C. 47 Julius Caesar made Antipater, a “wily Idumaean,” procurator of Judea, who divided his territories between his four sons, Galilee falling to the lot of Herod, who was afterwards appointed tetrarch of Judea by Mark Antony (B.C. 40), and also king of Judea by the Roman senate.
 He was of a stern and cruel disposition. “He was brutish and a stranger to all humanity.” Alarmed by the tidings of one “born King of the Jews,” he sent forth and “slew all the children that were in Bethlehem, and in all the coasts thereof, from two years old and under” (⟦40.2.16|마 2:16⟧). He was fond of splendour, and lavished great sums in rebuilding and adorning the cities of his empire. He rebuilt the city of Caesarea (q.v.) on the coast, and also the city of Samaria (q.v.), which he called Sebaste, in honour of Augustus. He restored the ruined temple of Jerusalem, a work which was begun B.C. 20, but was not finished till after Herod’s death, probably not till about A.D. 50 (⟦43.2.20|요 2:20⟧). After a troubled reign of thirty-seven years, he died at Jericho amid great agonies both of body and mind, B.C. 4, i.e., according to the common chronology, in the year in which Jesus was born.
 After his death his kingdom was divided among three of his sons. Of these, Philip had the land east of Jordan, between Caesarea Philippi and Bethabara, Antipas had Galilee and Peraea, while Archelaus had Judea and Samaria.

(⟦3.11.19|레 11:19⟧; ⟦5.14.18|신 14:18⟧), ranked among the unclean birds. The Hebrew name is ’anaphah, and indicates that the bird so named is remarkable for its angry disposition. “The herons are wading-birds, peculiarly irritable, remarkable for their voracity, frequenting marshes and oozy rivers, and spread over the regions of the East.” The Ardea russeta, or little golden egret, is the commonest species in Asia.

Intelligence, a city ruled over by Sihon, king of the Amorites (⟦6.3.10|수 3:10⟧; ⟦6.13.17|13:17⟧). It was taken by Moses (⟦4.21.23|민 21:23⟧), and became afterwards a Levitical city (⟦6.21.39|수 21:39⟧) in the tribe of Reuben (⟦4.32.37|민 32:37⟧). After the Exile it was taken possession of by the Moabites (⟦23.15.4|사 15:4⟧; ⟦24.48.2|렘 48:2⟧, ⟦24.48.34|34⟧, ⟦24.48.45|45⟧). The ruins of this town are still seen about 20 miles east of Jordan from the north end of the Dead Sea. There are reservoirs in this district, which are probably the “fishpools” referred to in ⟦22.7.4|아 7:4⟧.
Fatness, a town in the south of Judah (⟦6.15.27|수 15:27⟧).

Dread, a descendant of Canaan, and the ancestor of the Hittites (⟦1.10.18|창 10:18⟧; ⟦5.7.1|신 7:1⟧), who dwelt in the vicinity of Hebron (⟦1.23.3|창 23:3⟧, ⟦1.23.7|7⟧). The Hittites were a Hamitic race. They are called “the sons of Heth” (⟦1.23.3|창 23:3⟧, ⟦1.23.5|5⟧, ⟦1.23.7|7⟧, ⟦1.23.10|10⟧, ⟦1.23.16|16⟧, ⟦1.23.18|18⟧, ⟦1.23.20|20⟧).

Wrapped up, a place on the north border of Palestine. The “way of Hethlon” (⟦26.47.15|겔 47:15⟧; ⟦26.48.1|48:1⟧) is probably the pass at the end of Lebanon from the Mediterranean to the great plain of Hamath (q.v.), or the “entrance of Hamath.”

Whom Jehovah has strengthened.
1. Son of Ahaz (⟦12.18.1|왕하 18:1⟧; ⟦14.29.1|대하 29:1⟧), whom he succeeded on the throne of the kingdom of Judah. He reigned twenty-nine years (B.C. 726-697). The history of this king is contained in ⟦12.18.20|왕하 18:20⟧, ⟦23.36.1|사 36장⟧-39, and ⟦14.29.1|대하 29장⟧-32. He is spoken of as a great and good king. In public life he followed the example of his great-granfather Uzziah. He set himself to abolish idolatry from his kingdom, and among other things which he did for this end, he destroyed the “brazen serpent,” which had been removed to Jerusalem, and had become an object of idolatrous worship (⟦4.21.9|민 21:9⟧). A great reformation was wrought in the kingdom of Judah in his day (⟦12.18.4|왕하 18:4⟧; ⟦14.29.3|대하 29:3⟧).
 On the death of Sargon and the accession of his son Sennacherib to the throne of Assyria, Hezekiah refused to pay the tribute which his father had paid, and “rebelled against the king of Assyria, and served him not,” but entered into a league with Egypt (⟦23.30.1|사 30장⟧; ⟦23.31.1|31⟧; ⟦23.36.6|36:6⟧). This led to the invasion of Judah by Sennacherib (⟦12.18.13|왕하 18:13⟧), who took forty cities, and besieged Jerusalem with mounds. Hezekiah yielded to the demands of the Assyrian king, and agreed to pay him three hundred talents of silver and thirty of gold (18:14).
 But Sennacherib dealt treacherously with Hezekiah (⟦23.33.1|사 33:1⟧), and a second time within two years invaded his kingdom (⟦12.18.17|왕하 18:17⟧; ⟦14.32.9|대하 32:9⟧; ⟦23.36.1|사 36장⟧). This invasion issued in the destruction of Sennacherib’s army. Hezekiah prayed to God, and “that night the angel of the Lord went out, and smote in the camp of the Assyrians 185,000 men.” Sennacherib fled with the shattered remnant of his forces to Nineveh, where, seventeen years after, he was assassinated by his sons Adrammelech and Sharezer (⟦12.19.37|왕하 19:37⟧).
 The narrative of Hezekiah’s sickness and miraculous recovery is found in ⟦12.20.1|왕하 20:1⟧, ⟦12.20.2|2⟧ Chr. 32:24, ⟦23.38.1|사 38:1⟧. Various ambassadors came to congratulate him on his recovery, and among them Merodach-baladan, the viceroy of Babylon (⟦14.32.23|대하 32:23⟧; ⟦12.20.12|왕하 20:12⟧). He closed his days in peace and prosperity, and was succeeded by his son Manasseh. He was buried in the “chiefest of the sepulchres of the sons of David” (⟦14.32.27|대하 32:27⟧). He had “after him none like him among all the kings of Judah, nor any that were before him” (⟦12.18.5|왕하 18:5⟧).
Vision, the father of Tabrimon, and grandfather of Ben-hadad, king of Syria (⟦11.15.18|왕상 15:18⟧).

Swine or strong.
1. The head of the seventeenth course of the priests (⟦13.24.15|대상 24:15⟧).
2. ⟦16.10.20|느 10:20⟧, one who sealed Nehemiah’s covenant.
A Carmelite, one of David’s warriors (⟦13.11.37|대상 11:37⟧).

Enclosed.
1. One of the sons of Reuben (⟦1.46.9|창 46:9⟧; ⟦2.6.14|출 6:14⟧).
2. The older of the two sons of Pharez (⟦1.46.12|창 46:12⟧).
3. A plain in the south of Judah, west of Kadesh-barnea (⟦6.15.3|수 15:3⟧).
Rejoicing of Jehovah, one of David’s thirty-seven guards (⟦10.23.30|삼하 23:30⟧).

Called by the Accadians id Idikla; i.e., “the river of Idikla”, the third of the four rivers of Paradise (⟦1.2.14|창 2:14⟧). Gesenius interprets the word as meaning “the rapid Tigris.” The Tigris rises in the mountains of Armenia, 15 miles south of the source of the Euphrates, which, after pursuing a south-east course, it joins at Kurnah, about 50 miles above Bassorah. Its whole length is about 1,150 miles.

Life of (i.e., from) God, a native of Bethel, who built (i.e., fortified) Jericho some seven hundred years after its destruction by the Israelites. There fell on him for such an act the imprecation of Joshua (6:26). He laid the foundation in his first-born, and set up the gates in his youngest son (⟦11.16.34|왕상 16:34⟧), i.e., during the progress of the work all his children died.

Sacred city, a city of Phrygia, where was a Christian church under the care of Epaphras (⟦51.4.12|골 4:12⟧, ⟦51.4.13|13⟧). This church was founded at the same time as that of Colosse. It now bears the name of Pambuk-Kalek, i.e., “Cotton Castle”, from the white appearance of the cliffs at the base of which the ruins are found.

In ⟦19.92.3|시 92:3⟧ means the murmuring tone of the harp. In ⟦19.9.16|시 9:16⟧ it is a musical sign, denoting probably a pause in the instrumental interlude. In ⟦19.19.14|시 19:14⟧ the word is rendered “meditation;” and in ⟦25.3.62|애 3:62⟧, “device” (R.V., “imagination”).

An eminence, natural or artificial, where worship by sacrifice or offerings was made (⟦11.13.32|왕상 13:32⟧; ⟦12.17.29|왕하 17:29⟧). The first altar after the Flood was built on a mountain (⟦1.8.20|창 8:20⟧). Abraham also built an altar on a mountain (12:7, 8). It was on a mountain in Gilead that Laban and Jacob offered sacrifices (31:54). After the Israelites entered the Promised Land they were strictly enjoined to overthrow the high places of the Canaanites (⟦2.34.13|출 34:13⟧; ⟦5.7.5|신 7:5⟧; ⟦5.12.2|12:2⟧, ⟦5.12.3|3⟧), and they were forbidden to worship the Lord on high places (⟦5.12.11|신 12:11⟧), and were enjoined to use but one altar for sacrifices (⟦3.17.3|레 17:3⟧, ⟦3.17.4|4⟧; ⟦5.12.1|신 12장⟧; ⟦5.16.21|16:21⟧). The injunction against high places was, however, very imperfectly obeyed, and we find again and again mention made of them (⟦12.14.4|왕하 14:4⟧; ⟦12.15.4|15:4⟧, ⟦12.15.35|35⟧:⟦14.15.17|대하 15:17⟧, etc.).

Aaron was the first who was solemnly set apart to this office (⟦2.29.7|출 29:7⟧; ⟦2.30.23|30:23⟧; ⟦3.8.12|레 8:12⟧). He wore a peculiar dress, which on his death passed to his successor in office (⟦2.29.29|출 29:29⟧, ⟦2.29.30|30⟧). Besides those garments which he wore in common with all priests, there were four that were peculiar to himself as high priest:
1. The “robe” of the ephod, all of blue, of “woven work,” worn immediately under the ephod. It was without seam or sleeves. The hem or skirt was ornamented with pomegranates and golden bells, seventy-two of each in alternate order. The sounding of the bells intimated to the people in the outer court the time when the high priest entered into the holy place to burn incense before the Lord (⟦2.28.1|출 28장⟧).
2. The “ephod” consisted of two parts, one of which covered the back and the other the breast, which were united by the “curious girdle.” It was made of fine twined linen, and ornamented with gold and purple. Each of the shoulder-straps was adorned with a precious stone, on which the names of the twelve tribes were engraved. This was the high priest’s distinctive vestment (⟦9.2.28|삼상 2:28⟧; ⟦9.14.3|14:3⟧; ⟦9.21.9|21:9⟧; ⟦9.23.6|23:6⟧, ⟦9.23.9|9⟧; ⟦9.30.7|30:7⟧).
3. The “breastplate of judgment” (⟦2.28.6|출 28:6⟧, ⟦2.28.25|25-28⟧; ⟦2.39.2|39:2⟧) of “cunning work.” It was a piece of cloth doubled, of one span square. It bore twelve precious stones, set in four rows of three in a row, which constituted the Urim and Thummim (q.v.). These stones had the names of the twelve tribes engraved on them. When the high priest, clothed with the ephod and the breastplate, inquired of the Lord, answers were given in some mysterious way by the Urim and Thummim (⟦9.14.3|삼상 14:3⟧, ⟦9.14.18|18⟧, ⟦9.14.19|19⟧; 23:2, 4, 9, 11, 12; 28:6; ⟦10.5.23|삼하 5:23⟧).
4. The “mitre,” or upper turban, a twisted band of eight yards of fine linen coiled into a cap, with a gold plate in front, engraved with “Holiness to the Lord,” fastened to it by a ribbon of blue.
 To the high priest alone it was permitted to enter the holy of holies, which he did only once a year, on the great Day of Atonement, for “the way into the holiest of all was not yet made manifest” (⟦58.9.1|히 9장⟧; ⟦58.10.1|10⟧). Wearing his gorgeous priestly vestments, he entered the temple before all the people, and then, laying them aside and assuming only his linen garments in secret, he entered the holy of holies alone, and made expiation, sprinkling the blood of the sin offering on the mercy seat, and offering up incense. Then resuming his splendid robes, he reappeared before the people (⟦3.16.1|레 16장⟧). Thus the wearing of these robes came to be identified with the Day of Atonement.
 The office, dress, and ministration of the high priest were typical of the priesthood of our Lord (⟦58.4.14|히 4:14⟧; ⟦58.7.25|7:25⟧; ⟦58.9.12|9:12⟧, etc.).
 It is supposed that there were in all eighty-three high priests, beginning with Aaron (B.C. 1657) and ending with Phannias (A.D. 70). At its first institution the office of high priest was held for life (but comp. ⟦11.2.27|왕상 2:27⟧), and was hereditary in the family of Aaron (⟦4.3.10|민 3:10⟧). The office continued in the line of Eleazar, Aaron’s eldest son, for two hundred and ninety-six years, when it passed to Eli, the first of the line of Ithamar, who was the fourth son of Aaron. In this line it continued to Abiathar, whom Solomon deposed, and appointed Zadok, of the family of Eleazar, in his stead (⟦11.2.35|왕상 2:35⟧), in which it remained till the time of the Captivity. After the Return, Joshua, the son of Josedek, of the family of Eleazar, was appointed to this office. After him the succession was changed from time to time under priestly or political influences.

A raised road for public use. Such roads were not found in Palestine; hence the force of the language used to describe the return of the captives and the advent of the Messiah (⟦23.11.16|사 11:16⟧; ⟦23.35.8|35:8⟧; ⟦23.40.3|40:3⟧; ⟦23.62.10|62:10⟧) under the figure of the preparation of a grand thoroughfare for their march.
 During their possession of Palestine the Romans constructed several important highways, as they did in all countries which they ruled.

Portion of Jehovah.
1. ⟦13.6.54|대상 6:54⟧.
2. ⟦13.26.11|대상 26:11⟧.
3. The father of Eliakim (⟦12.18.18|왕하 18:18⟧, ⟦12.18.26|26⟧, ⟦12.18.37|37⟧).
4. The father of Gemariah (⟦24.29.3|렘 29:3⟧).
5. The father of the prophet Jeremiah (1:1).
6. The high priest in the reign of Josiah (⟦13.6.13|대상 6:13⟧; ⟦15.7.1|스 7:1⟧). To him and his deputy (⟦12.23.5|왕하 23:5⟧), along with the ordinary priests and the Levites who had charge of the gates, was entrusted the purification of the temple in Jerusalem. While this was in progress, he discovered in some hidden corner of the building a book called the “book of the law” (⟦12.22.8|왕하 22:8⟧) and the “book of the covenant” (23:2). Some have supposed that this “book” was nothing else than the original autograph copy of the Pentateuch written by Moses (⟦5.31.9|신 31:9⟧). This remarkable discovery occurred in the eighteenth year of Josiah’s reign (B.C. 624), a discovery which permanently affected the whole subsequent history of Israel.
7. ⟦16.12.7|느 12:7⟧.
8. ⟦16.8.4|느 8:4⟧.

1. Heb. gib’eah, a curved or rounded hill, such as are common to Palestine (⟦19.65.12|시 65:12⟧; ⟦19.72.3|72:3⟧; ⟦19.114.4|114:4⟧, ⟦19.114.6|6⟧).
2. Heb. har, properly a mountain range rather than an individual eminence (⟦2.24.4|출 24:4⟧, ⟦2.24.12|12⟧, ⟦2.24.13|13⟧, ⟦2.24.18|18⟧; ⟦4.14.40|민 14:40⟧, ⟦4.14.44|44⟧, ⟦4.14.45|45⟧). In ⟦5.1.7|신 1:7⟧, ⟦6.9.1|수 9:1⟧; ⟦6.10.40|10:40⟧; ⟦6.11.16|11:16⟧, it denotes the elevated district of Judah, Benjamin, and Ephraim, which forms the watershed between the Mediterranean and the Dead Sea.
3. Heb. ma’aleh in ⟦9.9.11|삼상 9:11⟧. Authorized Version “hill” is correctly rendered in the Revised Version “ascent.”
4. In ⟦42.9.37|눅 9:37⟧ the “hill” is the Mount of Transfiguration.
Praising, a Pirathonite, father of the judge Abdon (⟦7.12.13|삿 12:13⟧, ⟦7.12.15|15⟧).
On the south of the Valley of Hinnom. It is so called from a tradition that the house of the high priest Caiaphas, when the rulers of the Jews resolved to put Christ to death, stood here.

Heb. ‘ayalah (⟦10.22.34|삼하 22:34⟧; ⟦19.18.33|시 18:33⟧, etc.) and ‘ayeleth (⟦19.22.1|시 22편⟧, title), the female of the hart or stag. It is referred to as an emblem of activity (⟦1.49.21|창 49:21⟧), gentleness (⟦20.5.19|잠 5:19⟧), feminine modesty (⟦22.2.7|아 2:7⟧; ⟦22.3.5|3:5⟧), earnest longing (⟦19.42.1|시 42:1⟧), timidity (⟦19.29.9|시 29:9⟧). In the title of ⟦19.22.1|시 22편⟧, the word probably refers to some tune bearing that name.

(Heb. tsir), that on which a door revolves. “Doors in the East turn rather on pivots than on what we term hinges. In Syria, and especially in the Hauran, there are many ancient doors, consisting of stone slabs with pivots carved out of the same piece inserted in sockets above and below, and fixed during the building of the house” (⟦20.26.14|잠 26:14⟧).

A deep, narrow ravine separating Mount Zion from the so-called “Hill of Evil Counsel.” It took its name from “some ancient hero, the son of Hinnom.” It is first mentioned in ⟦6.15.8|수 15:8⟧. It had been the place where the idolatrous Jews burned their children alive to Moloch and Baal. A particular part of the valley was called Tophet, or the “fire-stove,” where the children were burned. After the Exile, in order to show their abhorrence of the locality, the Jews made this valley the receptacle of the offal of the city, for the destruction of which a fire was, as is supposed, kept constantly burning there.
 The Jews associated with this valley these two ideas, (1) that of the sufferings of the victims that had there been sacrificed; and (2) that of filth and corruption. It became thus to the popular mind a symbol of the abode of the wicked hereafter. It came to signify hell as the place of the wicked. “It might be shown by infinite examples that the Jews expressed hell, or the place of the damned, by this word. The word Gehenna [the Greek contraction of Hinnom] was never used in the time of Christ in any other sense than to denote the place of future punishment.” About this fact there can be no question. In this sense the word is used eleven times in our Lord’s discourses (⟦40.23.33|마 23:33⟧; ⟦42.12.5|눅 12:5⟧; ⟦40.5.22|마 5:22⟧, etc.).

High-born.
1. Generally “Huram,” one of the sons of Bela (⟦13.8.5|대상 8:5⟧).
2. Also “Huram” and “Horam,” king of Tyre. He entered into an alliance with David, and assisted him in building his palace by sending him able workmen, and also cedar-trees and fir-trees from Lebanon (⟦10.5.11|삼하 5:11⟧; ⟦13.14.1|대상 14:1⟧). After the death of David he entered into a similar alliance with Solomon, and assisted him greatly in building the temple (⟦11.5.1|왕상 5:1⟧; ⟦11.9.11|9:11⟧; ⟦14.2.3|대하 2:3⟧). He also took part in Solomon’s traffic to the Eastern Seas (⟦11.9.27|왕상 9:27⟧; ⟦11.10.11|10:11⟧; ⟦14.8.18|대하 8:18⟧; ⟦14.9.10|9:10⟧).
3. The “master workman” whom Hiram sent to Solomon. He was the son of a widow of Dan, and of a Tyrian father. In ⟦14.2.13|대하 2:13⟧ “Huram my father” should be Huram Abi, the word “Abi” (rendered here “my father”) being regarded as a proper name, or it may perhaps be a title of distinction given to Huram, and equivalent to “master.” (Comp. ⟦11.7.14|왕상 7:14⟧; ⟦14.4.16|대하 4:16⟧.) He cast the magnificent brazen works for Solomon’s temple in clay-beds in the valley of Jordan, between Succoth and Zarthan.

A labourer employed on hire for a limited time (⟦18.7.1|욥 7:1⟧; ⟦18.14.6|14:6⟧; ⟦41.1.20|막 1:20⟧). His wages were paid as soon as his work was over (⟦3.19.13|레 19:13⟧). In the time of our Lord a day’s wage was a “penny” (q.v.) i.e., a Roman denarius (⟦40.20.1|마 20:1⟧).

To express contempt (⟦18.27.23|욥 27:23⟧). The destruction of the temple is thus spoken of (⟦11.9.8|왕상 9:8⟧). Zechariah (10:8) speaks of the Lord gathering the house of Judah as it were with a hiss: “I will hiss for them.” This expression may be “derived from the noise made to attract bees in hiving, or from the sound naturally made to attract a person’s attention.”

Palestine and Syria appear to have been originally inhabited by three different tribes.
1. The Semites, living on the east of the isthmus of Suez. They were nomadic and pastoral tribes.
2. The Phoenicians, who were merchants and traders; and
3. the Hittites, who were the warlike element of this confederation of tribes. They inhabited the whole region between the Euphrates and Damascus, their chief cities being Carchemish on the Euphrates, and Kadesh, now Tell Neby Mendeh, in the Orontes valley, about six miles south of the Lake of Homs. These Hittites seem to have risen to great power as a nation, as for a long time they were formidable rivals of the Egyptian and Assyrian empires. In the book of Joshua they always appear as the dominant race to the north of Galilee.
 Somewhere about the twenty-third century B.C. the Syrian confederation, led probably by the Hittites, arched against Lower Egypt, which they took possession of, making Zoan their capital. Their rulers were the Hyksos, or shepherd kings. They were at length finally driven out of Egypt. Rameses II. sought vengeance against the “vile Kheta,” as he called them, and encountered and defeated them in the great battle of Kadesh, four centuries after Abraham.
 They are first referred to in Scripture in the history of Abraham, who bought from Ephron the Hittite the field and the cave of Machpelah (⟦1.15.20|창 15:20⟧: 23:3-18). They were then settled at Kirjath-arba. From this tribe Esau took his first two wives (26:34; 36:2).
 They are afterwards mentioned in the usual way among the inhabitants of the Promised Land (⟦2.23.28|출 23:28⟧). They were closely allied to the Amorites, and are frequently mentioned along with them as inhabiting the mountains of Palestine. When the spies entered the land they seem to have occupied with the Amorites the mountain region of Judah (⟦4.13.29|민 13:29⟧). They took part with the other Canaanites against the Israelites (⟦6.9.1|수 9:1⟧; ⟦6.11.3|11:3⟧).
 After this there are few references to them in Scripture. Mention is made of “Ahimelech the Hittite” (⟦9.26.6|삼상 26:6⟧), and of “Uriah the Hittite,” one of David’s chief officers (⟦10.23.39|삼하 23:39⟧; ⟦13.11.41|대상 11:41⟧). In the days of Solomon they were a powerful confederation in the north of Syria, and were ruled by “kings.” They are met with after the Exile still a distinct people (⟦15.9.1|스 9:1⟧; comp. ⟦16.13.23|느 13:23⟧).
 The Hebrew merchants exported horses from Egypt not only for the kings of Israel, but also for the Hittites (⟦11.10.28|왕상 10:28⟧, ⟦11.10.29|29⟧). From the Egyptian monuments we learn that “the Hittites were a people with yellow skins and ‘Mongoloid’ features, whose receding foreheads, oblique eyes, and protruding upper jaws are represented as faithfully on their own monuments as they are on those of Egypt, so that we cannot accuse the Egyptian artists of caricaturing their enemies. The Amorites, on the contrary, were a tall and handsome people. They are depicted with white skins, blue eyes, and reddish hair, all the characteristics, in fact, of the white race” (Sayce’s The Hittites). The original seat of the Hittite tribes was the mountain ranges of Taurus. They belonged to Asia Minor, and not to Syria.

One of the original tribes scattered over Palestine, from Hermon to Gibeon in the south. The name is interpreted as “midlanders” or “villagers” (⟦1.10.17|창 10:17⟧; ⟦13.1.15|대상 1:15⟧). They were probably a branch of the Hittites. At the time of Jacob’s return to Canaan, Hamor the Hivite was the “prince of the land” (⟦1.24.2|창 24:2⟧).
 They are next mentioned during the Conquest (⟦6.9.7|수 9:7⟧; ⟦6.11.19|11:19⟧). They principally inhabited the northern confines of Western Palestine (⟦6.11.3|수 11:3⟧; ⟦7.3.3|삿 3:3⟧). A remnant of them still existed in the time of Solomon (⟦11.9.20|왕상 9:20⟧).
An ancestor of the prophet Zephaniah (1:1).

Beloved, the Kenite, has been usually identified with Jethro (q.v.), ⟦2.18.5|출 18:5⟧, ⟦2.18.27|27⟧; comp. ⟦4.10.29|민 10:29⟧, ⟦4.10.30|30⟧. In ⟦7.4.11|삿 4:11⟧, the word rendered “father-in-law” means properly any male relative by marriage (comp. ⟦1.19.14|창 19:14⟧, “son-in-law,” A.V.), and should be rendered “brother-in-law,” as in the R.V. His descendants followed Israel to Canaan (⟦4.10.29|민 10:29⟧), and at first pitched their tents near Jericho, but afterwards settled in the south in the borders of Arad (⟦7.1.8|삿 1:8⟧, ⟦7.1.16|16⟧).
Hiding-place, a place to the north of Damascus, to which Abraham pursued Chedorlaomer and his confederates (⟦1.14.15|창 14:15⟧).

Majesty of Jehovah.
1. One of the Levites who assisted Ezra in expounding the law (⟦16.8.7|느 8:7⟧; ⟦16.9.5|9:5⟧).
2. ⟦16.10.18|느 10:18⟧, a Levite who sealed the covenant.
Partridge, one of the daughters of Zelophehad the Gileadite, to whom portions were assigned by Moses (⟦4.26.33|민 26:33⟧; ⟦4.27.1|27:1⟧; ⟦4.36.11|36:11⟧).
Jehovah impels, the king of Hebron who joined the league against Gibeon. He and his allies were defeated (⟦6.10.3|수 10:3⟧, ⟦6.10.5|5⟧, ⟦6.10.16|16⟧-27).
A fortress, the name given to David’s lurking-places (⟦9.22.4|삼상 22:4⟧, ⟦9.22.5|5⟧; ⟦9.24.22|24:22⟧).

In the highest sense belongs to God (⟦23.6.3|사 6:3⟧; ⟦66.15.4|계 15:4⟧), and to Christians as consecrated to God’s service, and in so far as they are conformed in all things to the will of God (⟦45.6.19|롬 6:19⟧, ⟦45.6.22|22⟧; ⟦49.1.4|엡 1:4⟧; ⟦56.1.8|딛 1:8⟧; ⟦60.1.15|벧전 1:15⟧). Personal holiness is a work of gradual development. It is carried on under many hindrances, hence the frequent admonitions to watchfulness, prayer, and perseverance (⟦46.1.30|고전 1:30⟧; ⟦47.7.1|고후 7:1⟧; ⟦49.4.23|엡 4:23⟧, ⟦49.4.24|24⟧).

The third Person of the adorable Trinity.
 His personality is proved (1) from the fact that the attributes of personality, as intelligence and volition, are ascribed to him (⟦43.14.17|요 14:17⟧, ⟦43.14.26|26⟧; 15:26; ⟦46.2.10|고전 2:10⟧, ⟦46.2.11|11⟧; 12:11). He reproves, helps, glorifies, intercedes (⟦43.16.7|요 16:7⟧; ⟦45.8.26|롬 8:26⟧). (2) He executes the offices peculiar only to a person. The very nature of these offices involves personal distinction (⟦42.12.12|눅 12:12⟧; ⟦44.5.32|행 5:32⟧; ⟦44.15.28|15:28⟧; ⟦44.16.6|16:6⟧; ⟦44.28.25|28:25⟧; ⟦46.2.13|고전 2:13⟧; ⟦58.2.4|히 2:4⟧; ⟦58.3.7|3:7⟧; 2 Pet. 1:21).
 His divinity is established (1) from the fact that the names of God are ascribed to him (⟦2.17.7|출 17:7⟧; ⟦19.95.7|시 95:7⟧; comp. ⟦58.3.7|히 3:7⟧); and (2) that divine attributes are also ascribed to him, omnipresence (⟦19.139.7|시 139:7⟧; ⟦49.2.17|엡 2:17⟧, ⟦49.2.18|18⟧; ⟦46.12.13|고전 12:13⟧); omniscience (⟦46.2.10|고전 2:10⟧, ⟦46.2.11|11⟧); omnipotence (⟦42.1.35|눅 1:35⟧; ⟦45.8.11|롬 8:11⟧); eternity (⟦58.9.4|히 9:4⟧). (3) Creation is ascribed to him (⟦1.1.2|창 1:2⟧; ⟦18.26.13|욥 26:13⟧; ⟦19.104.30|시 104:30⟧), and the working of miracles (⟦40.12.28|마 12:28⟧; ⟦46.12.9|고전 12:9⟧). (4) Worship is required and ascribed to him (⟦23.6.3|사 6:3⟧; ⟦44.28.25|행 28:25⟧; ⟦45.9.1|롬 9:1⟧; ⟦66.1.4|계 1:4⟧; ⟦40.28.19|마 28:19⟧).

The second or interior portion of the tabernacle. It was left in total darkness. No one was permitted to enter it except the high priest, and that only once a year. It contained the ark of the covenant only (⟦2.25.10|출 25:10⟧). It was in the form of a perfect cube of 20 cubits.

One of the two portions into which the tabernacle was divided (⟦2.26.31|출 26:31⟧; ⟦2.37.17|37:17⟧; ⟦58.9.2|히 9:2⟧). It was 20 cubits long and 10 in height and breadth. It was illuminated by the golden candlestick, as it had no opening to admit the light. It contained the table of showbread (⟦2.25.23|출 25:23⟧) and the golden altar of incense (30:1-11). It was divided from the holy of holies by a veil of the most costly materials and the brightest colours.
 The arrangement of the temple (q.v.) was the same in this respect. In it the walls of hewn stone were wainscotted with cedar and overlaid with gold, and adorned with beautiful carvings. It was entered from the porch by folding doors overlaid with gold and richly embossed. Outside the holy place stood the great tank or “sea” of molten brass, supported by twelve oxen, three turned each way, capable of containing two thousand baths of water. Besides this there were ten lavers and the brazen altar of burnt sacrifice.

Heap, the largest of dry measures, containing about 8 bushels or 1 quarter English = 10 ephahs (⟦3.27.16|레 27:16⟧; ⟦4.11.32|민 11:32⟧) = a COR.
 “Half a homer,” a grain measure mentioned only in ⟦28.3.2|호 3:2⟧.

1. Heb. ya’ar, occurs only ⟦9.14.25|삼상 14:25⟧, ⟦9.14.27|27⟧, ⟦9.14.29|29⟧; ⟦22.5.1|아 5:1⟧, where it denotes the honey of bees. Properly the word signifies a forest or copse, and refers to honey found in woods.
2. Nopheth, honey that drops (⟦19.19.10|시 19:10⟧; ⟦20.5.3|잠 5:3⟧; ⟦22.4.11|아 4:11⟧).
3. Debash denotes bee-honey (⟦7.14.8|삿 14:8⟧); but also frequently a vegetable honey distilled from trees (⟦1.43.11|창 43:11⟧; ⟦26.27.17|겔 27:17⟧). In these passages it may probably mean “dibs,” or syrup of grapes, i.e., the juice of ripe grapes boiled down to one-third of its bulk.
4. Tsuph, the cells of the honey-comb full of honey (⟦20.16.24|잠 16:24⟧; ⟦19.19.10|시 19:10⟧).
5. “Wild honey” (⟦40.3.4|마 3:4⟧) may have been the vegetable honey distilled from trees, but rather was honey stored by bees in rocks or in trees (⟦5.32.13|신 32:13⟧; ⟦19.81.16|시 81:16⟧; ⟦9.14.25|삼상 14:25⟧).
 Canaan was a “land flowing with milk and honey” (⟦2.3.8|출 3:8⟧). Milk and honey were among the chief dainties in the earlier ages, as they are now among the Bedawin; and butter and honey are also mentioned among articles of food (⟦23.7.15|사 7:15⟧). The ancients used honey instead of sugar (⟦19.119.103|시 119:103⟧; ⟦20.24.13|잠 24:13⟧); but when taken in great quantities it caused nausea, a fact referred to in ⟦20.25.16|잠 25:16⟧, ⟦20.25.17|17⟧ to inculcate moderation in pleasures. Honey and milk also are put for sweet discourse (⟦22.4.11|아 4:11⟧).
(Heb. tsaniph) a tiara round the head (⟦23.3.23|사 3:23⟧; R.V., pl., “turbans”). Rendered “diadem,” ⟦18.29.14|욥 29:14⟧; high priest’s “mitre,” ⟦38.3.5|슥 3:5⟧; “royal diadem,” ⟦23.62.3|사 62:3⟧.

A cleft hoof as of neat cattle (⟦2.10.26|출 10:26⟧; ⟦26.32.13|겔 32:13⟧); hence also of the horse, though not cloven (⟦23.5.28|사 5:28⟧). The “parting of the hoof” is one of the distinctions between clean and unclean animals (⟦3.11.3|레 11:3⟧; ⟦5.14.7|신 14:7⟧).

1. Heb. hah, a “ring” inserted in the nostrils of animals to which a cord was fastened for the purpose of restraining them (⟦12.19.28|왕하 19:28⟧; ⟦23.37.28|사 37:28⟧, ⟦23.37.29|29⟧; ⟦26.29.4|겔 29:4⟧; ⟦26.38.4|38:4⟧). “The Orientals make use of this contrivance for curbing their work-beasts...When a beast becomes unruly they have only to draw the cord on one side, which, by stopping his breath, punishes him so effectually that after a few repetitions he fails not to become quite tractable whenever he begins to feel it” (Michaelis). So God’s agents are never beyond his control.
2. Hakkah, a fish “hook” (⟦18.41.2|욥 41:2⟧, Heb. Text, 40:25; ⟦23.19.8|사 19:8⟧; ⟦35.1.15|합 1:15⟧).
3. Vav, a “peg” on which the curtains of the tabernacle were hung (⟦2.26.32|출 26:32⟧).
4. Tsinnah, a fish-hooks (⟦30.4.2|암 4:2⟧).
5. Mazleg, flesh-hooks (⟦9.2.13|삼상 2:13⟧, ⟦9.2.14|14⟧), a kind of fork with three teeth for turning the sacrifices on the fire, etc.
6. Mazmeroth, pruning-hooks (⟦23.2.4|사 2:4⟧; ⟦29.3.10|욜 3:10⟧).
7. ‘Agmon (⟦18.41.2|욥 41:2⟧, Heb. Text 40:26), incorrectly rendered in the Authorized Version. Properly a rush-rope for binding animals, as in Revised Version margin.

One of the three main elements of Christian character (⟦46.13.13|고전 13:13⟧). It is joined to faith and love, and is opposed to seeing or possessing (⟦45.8.24|롬 8:24⟧; ⟦62.3.2|요일 3:2⟧). “Hope is an essential and fundamental element of Christian life, so essential indeed, that, like faith and love, it can itself designate the essence of Christianity (⟦60.3.15|벧전 3:15⟧; ⟦58.10.23|히 10:23⟧). In it the whole glory of the Christian vocation is centred (⟦49.1.18|엡 1:18⟧; ⟦49.4.4|4:4⟧).” Unbelievers are without this hope (⟦49.2.12|엡 2:12⟧; ⟦52.4.13|살전 4:13⟧). Christ is the actual object of the believer’s hope, because it is in his second coming that the hope of glory will be fulfilled (⟦54.1.1|딤전 1:1⟧; ⟦51.1.27|골 1:27⟧; ⟦56.2.13|딛 2:13⟧). It is spoken of as “lively”, i.e., a living, hope, a hope not frail and perishable, but having a perennial life (⟦60.1.3|벧전 1:3⟧). In ⟦45.5.2|롬 5:2⟧ the “hope” spoken of is probably objective, i.e., “the hope set before us,” namely, eternal life (comp. 12:12). In ⟦62.3.3|요일 3:3⟧ the expression “hope in him” ought rather to be, as in the Revised Version, “hope on him,” i.e., a hope based on God.

Pugilist or client, one of the two sons of Eli, the high priest (⟦9.1.3|삼상 1:3⟧; ⟦9.2.34|2:34⟧), who, because he was “very old,” resigned to them the active duties of his office. By their scandalous conduct they brought down a curse on their father’s house (2:22, 12-27, 27-36; 3:11-14). For their wickedness they were called “sons of Belial,” i.e., worthless men (2:12). They both perished in the disastrous battle with the Philistines at Aphek (4:11).
I.e., PHARAOH-HOPHRA (called Apries by the Greek historian Herodotus) king of Egypt (B.C. 591-572) in the time of Zedekiah, king of Judah (⟦24.37.5|렘 37:5⟧ 44:30; ⟦26.29.6|겔 29:6⟧, ⟦26.29.7|7⟧).

Mountain.
1. One of the mountains of the chain of Seir or Edom, on the confines of Idumea (⟦4.20.22|민 20:22⟧; ⟦4.33.37|33:37⟧). It was one of the stations of the Israelites in the wilderness (33:37), which they reached in the circuitous route they were obliged to take because the Edomites refused them a passage through their territory. It was during the encampment here that Aaron died (⟦4.33.37|민 33:37⟧). The Israelites passed this mountain several times in their wanderings. It bears the modern name of Jebel Harun, and is the highest and most conspicious of the whole range. It stands about midway between the Dead Sea and the Elanitic gulf. It has two summits, in the hallow between which it is supposed that Aaron died. Others, however, suppose that this mountain is the modern Jebel Madurah, on the opposite, i.e., the western, side of the Arabah.
2. One of the marks of the northern boundary of Palestine (⟦4.34.7|민 34:7⟧, ⟦4.34.8|8⟧). Nowhere else mentioned. Perhaps it is one of the peaks of Lebanon.

Desert or mountain of the dried-up ground, a general name for the whole mountain range of which Sinai was one of the summits (⟦2.3.1|출 3:1⟧; ⟦2.17.6|17:6⟧; ⟦2.33.6|33:6⟧; ⟦19.106.19|시 106:19⟧, etc.). The modern name of the whole range is Jebel Musa. It is a huge mountain block, about 2 miles long by about 1 in breadth, with a very spacious plain at its north-east end, called the Er Rahah, in which the Israelites encamped for nearly a whole year.
Consecrated, one of the fenced cities of Naphtali (⟦6.19.38|수 19:38⟧).

Cave-men, a race of Troglodytes who dwelt in the limestone caves which abounded in Edom. Their ancestor was “Seir,” who probably gave his name to the district where he lived. They were a branch of the Hivites (⟦1.14.6|창 14:6⟧; ⟦1.36.20|36:20⟧; ⟦13.1.38|대상 1:38⟧, ⟦13.1.39|39⟧). They were dispossessed by the descendants of Esau, and as a people gradually became extinct (⟦5.2.12|신 2:12⟧).

Banning; i.e., placing under a “ban,” or devoting to utter destruction. After the manifestation of God’s anger against the Israelites, on account of their rebellion and their murmurings when the spies returned to the camp at Kadesh, in the wilderness of Paran, with an evil report of the land, they quickly repented of their conduct, and presumed to go up “to the head of the mountain,” seeking to enter the Promised Land, but without the presence of the Lord, without the ark of the convenant, and without Moses. The Amalekites and the Canaanites came down and “smote and discomfited them even unto Hormah” (⟦4.14.45|민 14:45⟧). This place, or perhaps the watch-tower commanding it, was originally called Zephath (⟦7.1.17|삿 1:17⟧), the modern Sebaiteh. Afterwards (⟦4.21.1|민 21:1⟧) Arad, the king of the Canaanites, at the close of the wanderings, when the Israelites were a second time encamped at Kadesh, “fought against them, and took some of them prisoners.” But Israel vowed a vow unto the Lord utterly to destroy the cities of the Canaanites; they “banned” them, and hence the place was now called Hormah. But this “ban” was not fully executed till the time of Joshua, who finally conquered the king of this district, so that the ancient name Zephath became “Hormah” (⟦6.12.14|수 12:14⟧; ⟦7.1.17|삿 1:17⟧).

Trumpets were at first horns perforated at the tip, used for various purposes (⟦6.6.4|수 6:4⟧, ⟦6.6.5|5⟧).
 Flasks or vessels were made of horn (⟦9.16.1|삼상 16:1⟧, ⟦9.16.13|13⟧; ⟦11.1.39|왕상 1:39⟧).
 But the word is used also metaphorically to denote the projecting corners of the altar of burnt offerings (⟦2.27.2|출 27:2⟧) and of incense (30:2). The horns of the altar of burnt offerings were to be smeared with the blood of the slain bullock (29:12; ⟦3.4.7|레 4:7⟧). The criminal, when his crime was accidental, found an asylum by laying hold of the horns of the altar (⟦11.1.50|왕상 1:50⟧; ⟦11.2.28|2:28⟧).
 The word also denotes the peak or summit of a hill (⟦23.5.1|사 5:1⟧, where the word “hill” is the rendering of the same Hebrew word).
 This word is used metaphorically also for strength (⟦5.33.17|신 33:17⟧) and honour (⟦18.16.15|욥 16:15⟧; ⟦25.2.3|애 2:3⟧). Horns are emblems of power, dominion, glory, and fierceness, as they are the chief means of attack and defence with the animals endowed with them (⟦27.8.5|단 8:5⟧, ⟦27.8.9|9⟧; ⟦9.2.1|삼상 2:1⟧; ⟦9.16.1|16:1⟧, ⟦9.16.13|13⟧; ⟦11.1.39|왕상 1:39⟧; ⟦11.22.11|22:11⟧; ⟦6.6.4|수 6:4⟧, ⟦6.6.5|5⟧; ⟦19.75.5|시 75:5⟧, ⟦19.75.10|10⟧; 132:17; ⟦42.1.69|눅 1:69⟧, etc.). The expression “horn of salvation,” applied to Christ, means a salvation of strength, or a strong Saviour (⟦42.1.69|눅 1:69⟧). To have the horn “exalted” denotes prosperity and triumph (⟦19.89.17|시 89:17⟧, ⟦19.89.24|24⟧). To “lift up” the horn is to act proudly (⟦38.1.21|슥 1:21⟧).
 Horns are also the symbol of royal dignity and power (⟦24.48.25|렘 48:25⟧; ⟦38.1.18|슥 1:18⟧; ⟦27.8.24|단 8:24⟧).

Heb. tsir’ah, “stinging”, (⟦2.23.28|출 23:28⟧; ⟦5.7.20|신 7:20⟧; ⟦6.24.12|수 24:12⟧). The word is used in these passages as referring to some means by which the Canaanites were to be driven out from before the Israelites. Some have supposed that the word is used in a metaphorical sense as the symbol of some panic which would seize the people as a “terror of God” (⟦1.35.5|창 35:5⟧), the consternation with which God would inspire the Canaanites. In Palestine there are four species of hornets, differing from our hornets, being larger in size, and they are very abundant. They “attack human beings in a very furious manner.” “The furious attack of a swarm of hornets drives cattle and horses to madness, and has even caused the death of the animals.”
Two caverns, a city of Moab to the south of the Arnon, built, apparently, upon an eminence, and a place of some importance (⟦23.15.5|사 15:5⟧; ⟦24.48.3|렘 48:3⟧, ⟦24.48.5|5⟧, ⟦24.48.34|34⟧).
The designation of Sanballat (⟦16.2.10|느 2:10⟧, ⟦16.2.19|19⟧), a native of Horonaim, or of one of the two Beth-horons, the “upper” or the “nether,” mentioned in ⟦6.16.3|수 16:3⟧, ⟦6.16.5|5⟧.

Always referred to in the Bible in connection with warlike operations, except ⟦23.28.28|사 28:28⟧. The war-horse is described ⟦18.39.19|욥 39:19⟧. For a long period after their settlement in Canaan the Israelites made no use of horses, according to the prohibition, ⟦5.17.16|신 17:16⟧. David was the first to form a force of cavalry (⟦10.8.4|삼하 8:4⟧). But Solomon, from his connection with Egypt, greatly multiplied their number (⟦11.4.26|왕상 4:26⟧; ⟦11.10.26|10:26⟧, ⟦11.10.29|29⟧). After this, horses were freely used in Israel (⟦11.22.4|왕상 22:4⟧; ⟦12.3.7|왕하 3:7⟧; ⟦12.9.21|9:21⟧, ⟦12.9.33|33⟧; ⟦12.11.16|11:16⟧). The furniture of the horse consisted simply of a bridle (⟦23.30.28|사 30:28⟧) and a curb (⟦19.32.9|시 32:9⟧).
A gate in the wall of Jerusalem, at the west end of the bridge, leading from Zion to the temple (⟦16.3.28|느 3:28⟧; ⟦24.31.40|렘 31:40⟧).

Occurs only in ⟦20.30.15|잠 30:15⟧ (Heb. ‘alukah); the generic name for any blood-sucking annelid. There are various species in the marshes and pools of Palestine. That here referred to, the Hoemopis, is remarkable for the coarseness of its bite, and is therefore not used for medical purposes. They are spoken of in the East with feelings of aversion and horror, because of their propensity to fasten on the tongue and nostrils of horses when they come to drink out of the pools. The medicinal leech (Hirudo medicinalis), besides other species of leeches, are common in the waters of Syria.

Heb. ba’al parash, “master of a horse.” The “horsemen” mentioned ⟦2.14.9|출 14:9⟧ were “mounted men”, i.e., men who rode in chariots. The army of Pharaoh consisted of a chariot and infantry force. We find that at a later period, however, the Egyptians had cavalry (⟦14.12.3|대하 12:3⟧).

Refuge.
1. A place on the border of the tribe of Asher (⟦6.19.29|수 19:29⟧), a little to the south of Zidon.
2. A Levite of the family of Merari (⟦13.16.38|대상 16:38⟧).
Save now! or Save, we beseech, (⟦40.21.9|마 21:9⟧). This was a customary form of acclamation at the feast of Tabernacles. (Comp. ⟦19.118.25|시 118:25⟧.)

Salvation, the son of Beeri, and author of the book of prophecies bearing his name. He belonged to the kingdom of Israel. “His Israelitish origin is attested by the peculiar, rough, Aramaizing diction, pointing to the northern part of Palestine; by the intimate acquaintance he evinces with the localities of Ephraim (5:1; 6:8, 9; 12:12; 14:6, etc.); by passages like 1:2, where the kingdom is styled ‘the land’, and 7:5, where the Israelitish king is designated as ‘our’ king.” The period of his ministry (extending to some sixty years) is indicated in the superscription (⟦28.1.1|호 1:1⟧, ⟦28.1.2|2⟧). He is the only prophet of Israel who has left any written prophecy.

This book stands first in order among the “Minor Prophets.” “The probable cause of the location of Hosea may be the thoroughly national character of his oracles, their length, their earnest tone, and vivid representations.” This was the longest of the prophetic books written before the Captivity. Hosea prophesied in a dark and melancholy period of Israel’s history, the period of Israel’s decline and fall. Their sins had brought upon them great national disasters. “Their homicides and fornication, their perjury and theft, their idolatry and impiety, are censured and satirized with a faithful severity.” He was a contemporary of Isaiah. The book may be divided into two parts, the first containing chapters 1-3, and symbolically representing the idolatry of Israel under imagery borrowed from the matrimonial relation. The figures of marriage and adultery are common in the Old Testament writings to represent the spiritual relations between Jehovah and the people of Israel. Here we see the apostasy of Israel and their punishment, with their future repentance, forgiveness, and restoration.
 The second part, containing 4-14, is a summary of Hosea’s discourses, filled with denunciations, threatenings, exhortations, promises, and revelations of mercy.
 Quotations from Hosea are found in ⟦40.2.15|마 2:15⟧; ⟦40.9.15|9:15⟧; ⟦40.12.7|12:7⟧; ⟦45.9.25|롬 9:25⟧, ⟦45.9.26|26⟧. There are, in addition, various allusions to it in other places (⟦42.23.30|눅 23:30⟧; ⟦66.6.16|계 6:16⟧, comp. ⟦28.10.8|호 10:8⟧; ⟦45.9.25|롬 9:25⟧, ⟦45.9.26|26⟧; ⟦60.2.10|벧전 2:10⟧, comp. ⟦28.1.10|호 1:10⟧, etc.).
 As regards the style of this writer, it has been said that “each verse forms a whole for itself, like one heavy toll in a funeral knell.” “Inversions (7:8; 9:11, 13; 12: 8), anacolutha (9:6; 12:8, etc.), ellipses (9:4; 13:9, etc.), paranomasias, and plays upon words, are very characteristic of Hosea (8:7; 9:15; 10:5; 11:5; 12:11).”

Salvation.
1. The original name of the son of Nun, afterwards called Joshua (⟦4.13.8|민 13:8⟧, ⟦4.13.16|16⟧; ⟦5.32.44|신 32:44⟧).
2. ⟦13.27.20|대상 27:20⟧. The ruler of Ephraim in David’s time.
3. The last king of Israel. He conspired against and slew his predecessor, Pekah (⟦23.7.16|사 7:16⟧), but did not ascend the throne till after an interregnum of warfare of eight years (⟦12.17.1|왕하 17:1⟧, ⟦12.17.2|2⟧). Soon after this he submitted to Shalmaneser, the Assyrian king, who a second time invaded the land to punish Hoshea, because of his withholding tribute which he had promised to pay. A second revolt brought back the Assyrian king Sargon, who besieged Samaria, and carried the ten tribes away beyond the Euphrates, B.C. 720 (⟦12.17.5|왕하 17:5⟧, ⟦12.17.6|6⟧; 18:9-12). No more is heard of Hoshea. He disappeared like “foam upon the water” (⟦28.10.7|호 10:7⟧; ⟦28.13.11|13:11⟧).

An entertainer (⟦45.16.23|롬 16:23⟧); a tavern-keeper, the keeper of a caravansary (⟦42.10.35|눅 10:35⟧).
 In warfare, a troop or military force. This consisted at first only of infantry. Solomon afterwards added cavalry (⟦11.4.26|왕상 4:26⟧; ⟦11.10.26|10:26⟧). Every male Israelite from twenty to fifty years of age was bound by the law to bear arms when necessary (⟦4.1.3|민 1:3⟧; ⟦4.26.2|26:2⟧; ⟦14.25.5|대하 25:5⟧).
 Saul was the first to form a standing army (⟦9.13.2|삼상 13:2⟧; ⟦9.24.2|24:2⟧). This example was followed by David (⟦13.27.1|대상 27:1⟧), and Solomon (⟦11.4.26|왕상 4:26⟧), and by the kings of Israel and Judah (⟦14.17.14|대하 17:14⟧; ⟦14.26.11|26:11⟧; ⟦12.11.4|왕하 11:4⟧, etc.).
A person delivered into the hands of another as a security for the performance of some promise, etc. (⟦12.14.14|왕하 14:14⟧; ⟦14.25.24|대하 25:24⟧).
To hamstring, i.e., sever the “tendon of Achilles” of the hinder legs of captured horses (⟦6.11.6|수 11:6⟧; ⟦10.8.4|삼하 8:4⟧; ⟦13.18.4|대상 18:4⟧), so as to render them useless.

First found in ⟦27.3.6|단 3:6⟧; ⟦27.4.19|4:19⟧, ⟦27.4.33|33⟧;⟦27.5.5|5:5⟧. It is the rendering of the Chaldee shaah, meaning a “moment,” a “look.” It is used in the New Testament frequently to denote some determinate season (⟦40.8.13|마 8:13⟧; ⟦42.12.39|눅 12:39⟧).
 With the ancient Hebrews the divisions of the day were “morning, evening, and noon-day” (⟦19.55.17|시 55:17⟧, etc.). The Greeks, following the Babylonians, divided the day into twelve hours. The Jews, during the Captivity, learned also from the Babylonians this method of dividing time. When Judea became subject to the Romans, the Jews adopted the Roman mode of reckoning time. The night was divided into four watches (⟦42.12.38|눅 12:38⟧; ⟦40.14.25|마 14:25⟧; ⟦40.13.25|13:25⟧). Frequent allusion is also made to hours (⟦40.25.13|마 25:13⟧; ⟦40.26.40|26:40⟧, etc.).
 An hour was the twelfth part of the day, reckoning from sunrise to sunset, and consequently it perpetually varied in length.

Till their sojourn in Egypt the Hebrews dwelt in tents. They then for the first time inhabited cities (⟦1.47.3|창 47:3⟧; ⟦2.12.7|출 12:7⟧; ⟦58.11.9|히 11:9⟧). From the earliest times the Assyrians and the Canaanites were builders of cities. The Hebrews after the Conquest took possession of the captured cities, and seem to have followed the methods of building that had been pursued by the Canaanites. Reference is made to the stone (⟦11.7.9|왕상 7:9⟧; ⟦23.9.10|사 9:10⟧) and marble (⟦13.29.2|대상 29:2⟧) used in building, and to the internal wood-work of the houses (⟦11.6.15|왕상 6:15⟧; ⟦11.7.2|7:2⟧; ⟦11.10.11|10:11⟧, ⟦11.10.12|12⟧; ⟦14.3.5|대하 3:5⟧; ⟦24.22.14|렘 22:14⟧). “Ceiled houses” were such as had beams inlaid in the walls to which wainscotting was fastened (⟦15.6.4|스 6:4⟧; ⟦24.22.14|렘 22:14⟧; ⟦37.1.4|학 1:4⟧). “Ivory houses” had the upper parts of the walls adorned with figures in stucco with gold and ivory (⟦11.22.39|왕상 22:39⟧; ⟦14.3.6|대하 3:6⟧; ⟦19.45.8|시 45:8⟧).
 The roofs of the dwelling-houses were flat, and are often alluded to in Scripture (⟦10.11.2|삼하 11:2⟧; ⟦23.22.1|사 22:1⟧; ⟦40.24.17|마 24:17⟧). Sometimes tents or booths were erected on them (⟦10.16.22|삼하 16:22⟧). They were protected by parapets or low walls (⟦5.22.8|신 22:8⟧). On the house-tops grass sometimes grew (⟦20.19.13|잠 19:13⟧; ⟦20.27.15|27:15⟧; ⟦19.129.6|시 129:6⟧, ⟦19.129.7|7⟧). They were used, not only as places of recreation in the evening, but also sometimes as sleeping-places at night (⟦9.9.25|삼상 9:25⟧, ⟦9.9.26|26⟧; ⟦10.11.2|삼하 11:2⟧; ⟦10.16.22|16:22⟧; ⟦27.4.29|단 4:29⟧; ⟦18.27.18|욥 27:18⟧; ⟦20.21.9|잠 21:9⟧), and as places of devotion (⟦24.32.29|렘 32:29⟧; ⟦24.19.13|19:13⟧).
Decreed, a town near Zebulun, not far from Jordan, on the border of Naphtali (⟦6.19.34|수 19:34⟧).
Circle, the second son of Aram (⟦1.10.23|창 10:23⟧), and grandson of Shem.

Weasel, a prophetess; the wife of Shallum. She was consulted regarding the “book of the law” discovered by the high priest Hilkiah (⟦12.22.14|왕하 22:14⟧; ⟦14.34.22|대하 34:22⟧). She resided in that part of Jerusalem called the Mishneh (A.V., “the college;” R.V., “the second quarter”), supposed by some to be the suburb between the inner and the outer wall, the second or lower city, Akra. Miriam (⟦2.15.20|출 15:20⟧) and Deborah (⟦7.4.4|삿 4:4⟧) are the only others who bear the title of “prophetess,” for the word in ⟦23.8.3|사 8:3⟧ means only the prophet’s wife.

A prominent Christian grace (⟦45.12.3|롬 12:3⟧; ⟦45.15.17|15:17⟧, ⟦45.15.18|18⟧; ⟦46.3.5|고전 3:5⟧; ⟦47.3.5|고후 3:5⟧; ⟦50.4.11|빌 4:11⟧). It is a state of mind well pleasing to God (⟦60.3.4|벧전 3:4⟧); it preserves the soul in tranquillity (⟦19.69.32|시 69:32⟧, ⟦19.69.33|33⟧), and makes us patient under trials (⟦18.1.22|욥 1:22⟧).
 Christ has set us an example of humility (⟦50.2.6|빌 2:6⟧). We should be led thereto by a remembrance of our sins (⟦25.3.39|애 3:39⟧), and by the thought that it is the way to honour (⟦20.16.18|잠 16:18⟧), and that the greatest promises are made to the humble (⟦19.147.6|시 147:6⟧; ⟦23.57.15|사 57:15⟧; ⟦23.66.2|66:2⟧; ⟦60.5.5|벧전 5:5⟧). It is a “great paradox in Christianity that it makes humility the avenue to glory.”

Mentioned first in ⟦1.10.9|창 10:9⟧ in connection with Nimrod. Esau was “a cunning hunter” (⟦1.25.27|창 25:27⟧). Hunting was practised by the Hebrews after their settlement in the “Land of Promise” (⟦3.17.15|레 17:15⟧; ⟦20.12.27|잠 12:27⟧). The lion and other ravenous beasts were found in Palestine (⟦9.17.34|삼상 17:34⟧; ⟦10.23.20|삼하 23:20⟧; ⟦11.13.24|왕상 13:24⟧; ⟦26.19.3|겔 19:3⟧), and it must have been necessary to hunt and destroy them. Various snares and gins were used in hunting (⟦19.91.3|시 91:3⟧; ⟦30.3.5|암 3:5⟧; ⟦10.23.20|삼하 23:20⟧).
 War is referred to under the idea of hunting (⟦24.16.16|렘 16:16⟧; ⟦26.32.30|겔 32:30⟧).

A hole, as of a viper, etc.
1. A son of Caleb (⟦13.2.19|대상 2:19⟧, ⟦13.2.50|50⟧; ⟦13.4.1|4:1⟧, ⟦13.4.4|4⟧; comp. ⟦14.1.5|대하 1:5⟧).
2. The husband of Miriam, Moses’ sister (⟦2.17.10|출 17:10⟧). He was associated with Aaron in charge of the people when Moses was absent on Sinai (⟦2.24.14|출 24:14⟧). He was probably of the tribe of Judah, and grandfather of Bezaleel (⟦2.31.2|출 31:2⟧; ⟦2.35.30|35:30⟧; ⟦13.2.19|대상 2:19⟧).
3. One of the five princes of Midian who were defeated and slain by the Israelites under the command of Phinehas (⟦4.31.8|민 31:8⟧).
Linen-worker, one of David’s heroes, a native of the valley of Mount Gaash (⟦13.11.32|대상 11:32⟧).

I.e., the “house-band,” connecting and keeping together the whole family. A man when betrothed was esteemed from that time a husband (⟦40.1.16|마 1:16⟧, ⟦40.1.20|20⟧; ⟦42.2.5|눅 2:5⟧). A recently married man was exempt from going to war for “one year” (⟦5.20.7|신 20:7⟧; ⟦5.24.5|24:5⟧).

One whose business it is to cultivate the ground. It was one of the first occupations, and was esteemed most honourable (⟦1.9.20|창 9:20⟧; ⟦1.26.12|26:12⟧, ⟦1.26.14|14⟧; ⟦1.37.7|37:7⟧, etc.). All the Hebrews, except those engaged in religious services, were husbandmen.

Quick, “the Archite,” “the king’s friend” (⟦13.27.33|대상 27:33⟧). When David fled from Jerusalem, on account of the rebellion of Absalom, and had reached the summit of Olivet, he there met Hushai, whom he sent back to Jerusalem for the purpose of counteracting the influence of Ahithophel, who had joined the ranks of Absalom (⟦10.15.32|삼하 15:32⟧, ⟦10.15.37|37⟧; 16:16-18). It was by his advice that Absalom refrained from immediately pursuing after David. By this delay the cause of Absalom was ruined, for it gave David time to muster his forces.

In ⟦4.6.4|민 6:4⟧ (Heb. zag) it means the “skin” of a grape. In ⟦12.4.42|왕하 4:42⟧ (Heb. tsiqlon) it means a “sack” for grain, as rendered in the Revised Version. In ⟦42.15.16|눅 15:16⟧, in the parable of the Prodigal Son, it designates the beans of the carob tree, or Ceratonia siliqua. From the supposition, mistaken, however, that it was on the husks of this tree that John the Baptist fed, it is called “St. John’s bread” and “locust tree.” This tree is in “February covered with innumerable purple-red pendent blossoms, which ripen in April and May into large crops of pods from 6 to 10 inches long, flat, brown, narrow, and bent like a horn (whence the Greek name keratia, meaning ‘little horns’), with a sweetish taste when still unripe. Enormous quantities of these are gathered for sale in various towns and for exportation.” “They were eaten as food, though only by the poorest of the poor, in the time of our Lord.” The bean is called a “gerah,” which is used as the name of the smallest Hebrew weight, twenty of these making a shekel.

Occurs only ⟦49.5.19|엡 5:19⟧ and ⟦51.3.16|골 3:16⟧. The verb to “sing an hymn” occurs ⟦40.26.30|마 26:30⟧ and ⟦41.14.26|막 14:26⟧. The same Greek word is rendered to “sing praises” ⟦44.16.25|행 16:25⟧ (R.V., “sing hymns”) and ⟦58.2.12|히 2:12⟧. The “hymn” which our Lord sang with his disciples at the last Supper is generally supposed to have been the latter part of the Hallel, comprehending ⟦19.113.1|시 113편⟧-118. It was thus a name given to a number of psalms taken together and forming a devotional exercise.
 The noun hymn is used only with reference to the services of the Greeks, and was distinguished from the psalm. The Greek tunes required Greek hymns. Our information regarding the hymnology of the early Christians is very limited.

One who puts on a mask and feigns himself to be what he is not; a dissembler in religion. Our Lord severely rebuked the scribes and Pharisees for their hypocrisy (⟦40.6.2|마 6:2⟧, ⟦40.6.5|5⟧, ⟦40.6.16|16⟧). “The hypocrite’s hope shall perish” (⟦18.8.13|욥 8:13⟧). The Hebrew word here rendered “hypocrite” rather means the “godless” or “profane,” as it is rendered in ⟦24.23.11|렘 23:11⟧, i.e., polluted with crimes.

(Heb. ‘ezob; LXX. hyssopos), first mentioned in ⟦2.12.22|출 12:22⟧ in connection with the institution of the Passover. We find it afterwards mentioned in ⟦3.14.4|레 14:4⟧, ⟦3.14.6|6⟧, ⟦3.14.52|52⟧; ⟦4.19.6|민 19:6⟧, ⟦4.19.18|18⟧; ⟦58.9.19|히 9:19⟧. It is spoken of as a plant “springing out of the wall” (⟦11.4.33|왕상 4:33⟧). Many conjectures have been formed as to what this plant really was. Some contend that it was a species of marjoram (origanum), six species of which are found in Palestine. Others with more probability think that it was the caper plant, the Capparis spinosa of Linnaeus. This plant grew in Egypt, in the desert of Sinai, and in Palestine. It was capable of producing a stem three or four feet in length (⟦40.27.48|마 27:48⟧; ⟦41.15.36|막 15:36⟧. Comp. ⟦43.19.29|요 19:29⟧).

People-waster, a city assigned to Manasseh (⟦6.17.11|수 17:11⟧), from which the Israelites, however, could not expel the Canaanites (⟦7.1.27|삿 1:27⟧). It is also called Bileam (⟦13.6.70|대상 6:70⟧). It was probably the modern Jelamah, a village 2 1/2 miles north of Jenin.
Illustrious, the tenth judge of Israel (⟦7.12.8|삿 12:8⟧). He ruled seven years.

When the tidings of the disastrous defeat of the Israelites in the battle against the Philistines near to Mizpeh were carried to Shiloh, the wife of Phinehas “was near to be delivered. And when she heard the tidings that the ark of God was taken, and that her father-in-law and her husband were dead, she bowed herself and travailed” (⟦9.4.19|삼상 4:19⟧). In her great distress she regarded not “the women that stood by her,” but named the child that was born “Ichabod” i.e., no glory, saying, “The glory is departed from Isreal;” and with that word on her lips she expired.

The capital of ancient Lycaonia. It was first visited by Paul and Barnabas from Antioch-in-Pisidia during the apostle’s first missionary journey (⟦44.13.50|행 13:50⟧, ⟦44.13.51|51⟧). Here they were persecuted by the Jews, and being driven from the city, they fled to Lystra. They afterwards returned to Iconium, and encouraged the church which had been founded there (14:21, 22). It was probably again visited by Paul during his third missionary journey along with Silas (18:23). It is the modern Konieh, at the foot of Mount Taurus, about 120 miles inland from the Mediterranean.
Snares(?), a city near the west border of Zebulun (⟦6.19.15|수 19:15⟧). It has been identified with the modern Jeida, in the valley of Kishon.

1. Timely (⟦13.6.21|대상 6:21⟧). A Gershonite Levite.
2. Lovely. The son of Zechariah (⟦13.27.21|대상 27:21⟧), the ruler of Manasseh in David’s time.
3. Timely. The father of Ahinadab, who was one of Solomon’s purveyors (⟦11.4.14|왕상 4:14⟧).
4. Lovely. A prophet of Judah who wrote the history of Rehoboam and Abijah (⟦14.12.15|대하 12:15⟧). He has been identified with Oded (⟦14.15.1|대하 15:1⟧).
5. Lovely. The father of Berachiah, and grandfather of the prophet Zechariah (⟦38.1.1|슥 1:1⟧, ⟦38.1.7|7⟧). He returned from Babylon (⟦16.12.4|느 12:4⟧).

1. Heb. aven, “nothingness;” “vanity” (⟦23.66.3|사 66:3⟧; ⟦23.41.29|41:29⟧; ⟦5.32.21|신 32:21⟧; ⟦11.16.13|왕상 16:13⟧; ⟦19.31.6|시 31:6⟧; ⟦24.8.19|렘 8:19⟧, etc.).
2. ‘Elil, “a thing of naught” (⟦19.97.7|시 97:7⟧; ⟦23.19.3|사 19:3⟧); a word of contempt, used of the gods of Noph (⟦26.30.13|겔 30:13⟧).
3. ‘Emah, “terror,” in allusion to the hideous form of idols (⟦24.50.38|렘 50:38⟧).
4. Miphletzeth, “a fright;” “horror” (⟦11.15.13|왕상 15:13⟧; ⟦14.15.16|대하 15:16⟧).
5. Bosheth, “shame;” “shameful thing” (⟦24.11.13|렘 11:13⟧; ⟦28.9.10|호 9:10⟧); as characterizing the obscenity of the worship of Baal.
6. Gillulim, also a word of contempt, “dung;” “refuse” (⟦26.16.36|겔 16:36⟧; ⟦26.20.8|20:8⟧; ⟦5.29.17|신 29:17⟧, marg.).
7. Shikkuts, “filth;” “impurity” (⟦26.37.23|겔 37:23⟧; ⟦34.3.6|나 3:6⟧).
8. Semel, “likeness;” “a carved image” (⟦5.4.16|신 4:16⟧).
9. Tselem, “a shadow” (⟦27.3.1|단 3:1⟧; ⟦9.6.5|삼상 6:5⟧), as distinguished from the “likeness,” or the exact counterpart.
10. Temunah, “similitude” (⟦5.4.12|신 4:12⟧). Here Moses forbids the several forms of Gentile idolatry.
11. ‘Atsab, “a figure;” from the root “to fashion,” “to labour;” denoting that idols are the result of man’s labour (⟦23.48.5|사 48:5⟧; ⟦19.139.24|시 139:24⟧, “wicked way;” literally, as some translate, “way of an idol”).
12. Tsir, “a form;” “shape” (⟦23.45.16|사 45:16⟧).
13. Matztzebah, a “statue” set up (⟦24.43.13|렘 43:13⟧); a memorial stone like that erected by Jacob (⟦1.28.18|창 28:18⟧; ⟦1.31.45|31:45⟧; ⟦1.35.14|35:14⟧, ⟦1.35.20|20⟧), by Joshua (4:9), and by Samuel (⟦9.7.12|삼상 7:12⟧). It is the name given to the statues of Baal (⟦12.3.2|왕하 3:2⟧; ⟦12.10.27|10:27⟧).
14. Hammanim, “sun-images.” Hamman is a synonym of Baal, the sun-god of the Phoenicians (⟦14.34.4|대하 34:4⟧, ⟦14.34.7|7⟧; 14:3, 5; ⟦23.17.8|사 17:8⟧).
15. Maskith, “device” (⟦3.26.1|레 26:1⟧; ⟦4.33.52|민 33:52⟧). In ⟦3.26.1|레 26:1⟧, the words “image of stone” (A.V.) denote “a stone or cippus with the image of an idol, as Baal, Astarte, etc.” In ⟦26.8.12|겔 8:12⟧, “chambers of imagery” (maskith), are “chambers of which the walls are painted with the figures of idols;” comp. ver. 10, 11.
16. Pesel, “a graven” or “carved image” (⟦23.44.10|사 44:10⟧). It denotes also a figure cast in metal (⟦5.7.25|신 7:25⟧; ⟦5.27.15|27:15⟧; ⟦23.40.19|사 40:19⟧; ⟦23.44.10|44:10⟧).
17. Massekah, “a molten image” (⟦5.9.12|신 9:12⟧; ⟦7.17.3|삿 17:3⟧, ⟦7.17.4|4⟧).
18. Teraphim, pl., “images,” family gods (penates) worshipped by Abram’s kindred (⟦6.24.14|수 24:14⟧). Put by Michal in David’s bed (⟦7.17.5|삿 17:5⟧; ⟦7.18.14|18:14⟧, ⟦7.18.17|17⟧, ⟦7.18.18|18⟧, ⟦7.18.20|20⟧; ⟦9.19.13|삼상 19:13⟧).
 “Nothing can be more instructive and significant than this multiplicity and variety of words designating the instruments and inventions of idolatry.”

Image-worship or divine honour paid to any created object. Paul describes the origin of idolatry in ⟦45.1.21|롬 1:21⟧: men forsook God, and sank into ignorance and moral corruption (1:28).
 The forms of idolatry are,
1. Fetishism, or the worship of trees, rivers, hills, stones, etc.
2. Nature worship, the worship of the sun, moon, and stars, as the supposed powers of nature.
3. Hero worship, the worship of deceased ancestors, or of heroes.
 In Scripture, idolatry is regarded as of heathen origin, and as being imported among the Hebrews through contact with heathen nations. The first allusion to idolatry is in the account of Rachel stealing her father’s teraphim (⟦1.31.19|창 31:19⟧), which were the relics of the worship of other gods by Laban’s progenitors “on the other side of the river in old time” (⟦6.24.2|수 24:2⟧). During their long residence in Egypt the Hebrews fell into idolatry, and it was long before they were delivered from it (⟦6.24.14|수 24:14⟧; ⟦26.20.7|겔 20:7⟧). Many a token of God’s displeasure fell upon them because of this sin.
 The idolatry learned in Egypt was probably rooted out from among the people during the forty years’ wanderings; but when the Jews entered Palestine, they came into contact with the monuments and associations of the idolatry of the old Canaanitish races, and showed a constant tendency to depart from the living God and follow the idolatrous practices of those heathen nations. It was their great national sin, which was only effectually rebuked by the Babylonian exile. That exile finally purified the Jews of all idolatrous tendencies.
 The first and second commandments are directed against idolatry of every form. Individuals and communities were equally amenable to the rigorous code. The individual offender was devoted to destruction (⟦2.22.20|출 22:20⟧). His nearest relatives were not only bound to denounce him and deliver him up to punishment (⟦5.13.18|신 13:18⟧), but their hands were to strike the first blow when, on the evidence of two witnesses at least, he was stoned (⟦5.17.2|신 17:2⟧). To attempt to seduce others to false worship was a crime of equal enormity (13:6-10). An idolatrous nation shared the same fate. No facts are more strongly declared in the Old Testament than that the extermination of the Canaanites was the punishment of their idolatry (⟦2.34.15|출 34:15⟧, ⟦2.34.16|16⟧; ⟦5.7.1|신 7장⟧; ⟦5.12.29|12:29⟧; ⟦5.20.17|20:17⟧), and that the calamities of the Israelites were due to the same cause (⟦24.2.17|렘 2:17⟧). “A city guilty of idolatry was looked upon as a cancer in the state; it was considered to be in rebellion, and treated according to the laws of war. Its inhabitants and all their cattle were put to death.” Jehovah was the theocratic King of Israel, the civil Head of the commonwealth, and therefore to an Israelite idolatry was a state offence (⟦9.15.23|삼상 15:23⟧), high treason. On taking possession of the land, the Jews were commanded to destroy all traces of every kind of the existing idolatry of the Canaanites (⟦2.23.24|출 23:24⟧, ⟦2.23.32|32⟧; 34:13; ⟦5.7.5|신 7:5⟧, ⟦5.7.25|25⟧; 12:1-3).
 In the New Testament the term idolatry is used to designate covetousness (⟦40.6.24|마 6:24⟧; ⟦42.16.13|눅 16:13⟧; ⟦51.3.5|골 3:5⟧; ⟦49.5.5|엡 5:5⟧).

Avengers.
1. ⟦4.13.7|민 13:7⟧, one of the spies of the tribe of Issachar.
2. Son of Nathan of Zobah, and one of David’s warriors (⟦10.23.36|삼하 23:36⟧).
3. ⟦13.3.22|대상 3:22⟧.

Ruins.
1. A city in the south of Judah (⟦6.15.29|수 15:29⟧).
2. One of the stations of the Israelites in the wilderness (⟦4.33.45|민 33:45⟧).
Ruins of Abarim, the forty-seventh station of the Israelites in the wilderness, “in the border of Moab” (⟦4.33.44|민 33:44⟧).

A ruin, a city of Naphtali, captured by Ben-hadad of Syria at the instance of Asa (⟦11.15.20|왕상 15:20⟧), and afterwards by Tiglath-pileser of Assyria (⟦12.15.29|왕하 15:29⟧) in the reign of Pekah; now el-Khiam.
An Ahohite, one of David’s chief warriors (⟦13.11.29|대상 11:29⟧); called also Zalmon (⟦10.23.28|삼하 23:28⟧).

A country to the north-west of Macedonia, on the eastern shores of the Adriatic, now almost wholly comprehended in Dalmatia, a name formerly given to the southern part of Illyricum (⟦55.4.10|딤후 4:10⟧). It was traversed by Paul in his third missionary journey (⟦45.15.19|롬 15:19⟧). It was the farthest district he had reached in preaching the gospel of Christ. This reference to Illyricum is in harmony with ⟦44.20.2|행 20:2⟧, inasmuch as the apostle’s journey over the parts of Macedonia would bring him to the borders of Illyricum.
Only in the phrase “chambers of his imagery” (⟦26.8.12|겔 8:12⟧).
Replenisher, the father of Micaiah the prophet (⟦14.18.7|대하 18:7⟧, ⟦14.18.8|8⟧).

God with us. In the Old Testament it occurs only in ⟦23.7.14|사 7:14⟧ and 8:8. Most Christian interpreters have regarded these words as directly and exclusively a prophecy of our Saviour, an interpretation borne out by the words of the evangelist Matthew (1:23).

Perpetuity of existence. The doctrine of immortality is taught in the Old Testament. It is plainly implied in the writings of Moses (⟦1.5.22|창 5:22⟧, ⟦1.5.24|24⟧; 25:8; 37:35; 47:9; 49:29, comp. ⟦58.11.13|히 11:13⟧; ⟦2.3.6|출 3:6⟧, comp. ⟦40.22.23|마 22:23⟧). It is more clearly and fully taught in the later books (⟦23.14.9|사 14:9⟧; ⟦19.17.15|시 17:15⟧; ⟦19.49.15|49:15⟧; ⟦19.73.24|73:24⟧). It was thus a doctrine obviously well known to the Jews.
 With the full revelation of the gospel this doctrine was “brought to light” (⟦55.1.10|딤후 1:10⟧; ⟦46.15.1|고전 15장⟧; ⟦47.5.1|고후 5:1⟧; ⟦52.4.13|살전 4:13⟧).

Is used to designate any action or word or thing as reckoned to a person. Thus in doctrinal language (1) the sin of Adam is imputed to all his descendants, i.e., it is reckoned as theirs, and they are dealt with therefore as guilty; (2) the righteousness of Christ is imputed to them that believe in him, or so attributed to them as to be considered their own; and (3) our sins are imputed to Christ, i.e., he assumed our “law-place,” undertook to answer the demands of justice for our sins. In all these cases the nature of imputation is the same (⟦45.5.12|롬 5:12⟧; comp. ⟦57.1.1|몬 1:1⟧:18, 19).

That act of grace whereby Christ took our human nature into union with his Divine Person, became man. Christ is both God and man. Human attributes and actions are predicated of him, and he of whom they are predicated is God.
